notes: Gets the main cases right: names are appended to the automate loader, global defaults reach them through a base policy, and internal names get the internal issuer. However, it copy-pastes the site-block split logic, adds an ad-hoc block that forces DefaultIssuers when cert_lifetime/http_port/https_port/default_bind are set (diverging from dummy-site-block output), and skips names covered by a wildcard site rather than an exact one; tests are thorough but encode those choices.

The main behaviour is implemented and the tests are thorough, but the split logic is duplicated inline and it always creates policies. It also adds an unrequested, ad hoc block that injects DefaultIssuers when cert_lifetime, http_port, https_port or default_bind is set, which makes the output differ from the site-block equivalent. It fails the hidden test.

Handles appending, the no-site-block case, internal splitting, http-only sites and auto_https off. It adds an unrequested heuristic where any hostless HTTPS site with non-empty settings suppresses all automate-name policies, uses wildcard coverage instead of exact matching, and duplicates the split logic (dropping the Tailscale handling); tests are reasonable but narrower.

The core feature works, but it duplicates the split logic inline and always creates a policy even with no global options. It adds a questionable 'custom catch-all' heuristic: any hostless site with non-empty automation settings stops listed names from getting their global-default policy, which contradicts 'as if they had a site block'. It fails the hidden test.

Cleanest of the three: it extracts the internal/public split into a reusable helper (preserving site-block behaviour), dedupes and sorts names, and builds a base policy so global options apply. It still deviates from the reference by skipping wildcard-covered names and always creating a policy, touches existing code via the refactor, and fails the hidden test; its tests cover the main spec bullets.

Parsing, the automate loader and internal-issuer handling work, and the inline split logic is cleanly factored into a reusable helper. However, it always creates a policy via newBaseAutomationPolicy(..., true), which leaves noisy empty policies for public names when internal names are also listed. It also skips names covered by a wildcard site, not only exact matches, so its output diverges from the reference and it fails the hidden test.
